clue.text: Game personnel in industrial area

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game
HR, human resources, is the personnel department

explanation.surface: Sports staff working in a manufacturing district.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ruhr is Germany's great coal and steel region, a byword for heavy industry.

clue.text: Tries again to go over brief

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to go over a part or a speech is to practise it

explanation.surface: Someone attempts something a second time to review a short document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like a noun, a lawyer's brief, but it tells you to cut the last letter. The definition is legal: a court that re-hears a case tries it again.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehear a case in court is to give it a second hearing, i.e. to try it again.

clue.text: Hex pretty much transformed web software

indicators.note: greatly changed in form, so the letters before it are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A curse that has been pretty much changed by some internet program.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty much' reads as a phrase meaning 'almost'; split it, and 'pretty' is fodder while 'much transformed' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypertext is the linked-text system underlying the World Wide Web and its pages.

clue.text: Get engrossed in homework with book pinched from female head?

definitions.note: read as 'get (someone) engrossed': a verb meaning to preoccupy

indicators.note: something pinched is stolen away, so the named letter is taken out of what follows

parts.note: prep is school homework in British usage
B is the abbreviation for book
a boss with the feminine ending -ess

explanation.surface: A pupil absorbed in homework after nicking a book from the headmistress.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove B from BOSSESS and add it to PREP. Prep is the British boarding-school word for homework.
explanation.definitionFit: To prepossess is to preoccupy the mind or to engross someone beforehand, so it is to get them engrossed.

clue.text: Crying over? That is the wrong way to keep in step!

indicators.note: to keep something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a rung is a step on a ladder

indicators.note: going the wrong way means running backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is'

explanation.surface: Someone sobbing over a failure, told that's the wrong way to march in time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crying over' is idiomatic: crying over spilt milk is regretting it. The exclamation mark is surface colour, a drill sergeant's rebuke.
explanation.definitionFit: Rueing something means regretting it, as in crying over spilt milk.

clue.text: Mary Jane and son drove a bit of an old crock

definitions.text: a bit of an old crock

parts.note: Mary Jane is slang for marijuana, i.e. pot
S is the abbreviation for son
a drove is a herd of animals being driven

explanation.surface: A woman and her son drove a decrepit old car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drove' reads as a past tense verb but is a noun; 'old crock' suggests a jalopy but means an ancient pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A potsherd is a broken fragment of ancient pottery, literally a piece of an old crock or jar.

clue.text: Instinctive, small worry: chap's out of breath a lot?

definitions.note: the phrase is usually 'by the seat of the pants', meaning by instinct

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
as in 'what's eating you?'
oft means often, a lot
the man, he, pants when breathless

explanation.surface: A man often short of breath acts on instinct while fretting a little.
explanation.walkthrough: Note the order: 'a lot' comes last in the clue but goes before HE PANTS. Flying by the seat of the pants means acting on instinct without plan.
explanation.definitionFit: Seat-of-the-pants describes action guided by instinct and feel rather than by planning or instruments.

clue.text: Ham, perhaps the ultimate in Tyrolese speck

indicators.note: the ultimate letter is the last one, so only the end of the next word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of Tyrolese
a mote is a tiny speck of dust

explanation.surface: Ham is perhaps the finest example of Tyrolean speck, a cured pork.
explanation.walkthrough: Speck is a smoked ham from the Tyrol, so the surface is about food; here 'ham' is a verb, to overact.
explanation.definitionFit: To ham it up is to overact, and to emote is to express feeling theatrically; hamming is one way of emoting.

clue.text: Key from student class finally changing hands

indicators.note: the last letter swaps one hand for the other, right becoming left

parts.note: a seminar is a small class for students

explanation.surface: A key passing between people at the end of a lecture group.
explanation.walkthrough: R (right) at the end of SEMINAR becomes L (left), swapping hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A seminal work is a key, highly influential one that shapes later developments.

clue.text: Sound of policeman thundered around walls of tenement

parts.note: copper is slang for a police officer

indicators.note: something around another encloses it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: to boom is to thunder

indicators.note: the walls of a building are its outsides, so only the outer letters of the next word are used

parts.note: first and last letters of tenement

explanation.surface: The noise a police officer makes thundering around the walls of a block of flats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound of' looks like a homophone signal; 'Sound' is the definition, an adjective meaning reliable, and 'of' merely links.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper-bottomed means thoroughly reliable, from ships sheathed in copper below the waterline, so it means sound.

clue.text: I lead in Polish part of leg

definitions.note: loosely: the hip bone sits at the top of the leg

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so these letters go within the following word

parts.note: to hone is to sharpen or polish
taken as written
Pb is the chemical symbol for lead

explanation.surface: Someone from Poland heading the team in some part of the leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' masquerades as a nationality at the start of a word; it is the verb. IPB goes in HONE after H.
explanation.definitionFit: The hip bone joins the thigh at the top of the leg, so it can loosely count as a part of it.

clue.text: European wearing tie at revolving restaurant

indicators.note: something revolving turns round, so the phrase is read from end to start

parts.note: to moor is to tie up a boat

indicators.note: the wearer surrounds what is worn, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European in a necktie at a rotating restaurant on a tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolving restaurant' reads as one phrase, but 'revolving' belongs to the wordplay and turns 'tie at' round before the European goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A tearoom is a small café or restaurant serving tea and light meals.

clue.text: Hardly anything mostly coin-operated worked with hand

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is cut off
worked as in kneaded or wrought, so the letters are reshaped into a new order

parts.note: the word without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A slot machine that hardly works, needing a hand to operate it.
explanation.walkthrough: Fodder spans the link 'with': trimmed COIN-OPERATE(D) plus HAND, fifteen letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop in the ocean is an idiom for an amount so tiny it makes no real difference.

clue.text: Mountains seen beyond delta in Highlands

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a jagged mountain range
second meaning: the letter that follows D in the word Highlands, named in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A view of peaks past a river mouth in the north of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: In HIGHLANDS the letter after D (delta) is S, and S in the NATO phonetic alphabet is Sierra. 'Delta' looks like a river mouth but is the code word for D.
explanation.definitionFit: Sierra is both a word for a range of saw-toothed peaks and the radio code word for the letter S.

clue.text: Not perhaps digging someone's grave

definitions.meaning: first meaning: disapproving; 'digging' is slang for liking, so not liking someone's work
second meaning: serious, at a turning point

explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a gravedigger; 'digging' is the slang for enjoying something, and 'grave' is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Critical means fault-finding, the opposite of approving, and also means grave or dangerously serious, as a patient's condition.

clue.text: Money and possibly passport to hold on to before getting dismissed

parts.note: cash is money

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it round, so these letters sit inside the next piece

parts.note: a passport is one example of ID
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: Cash and a passport kept back before someone is fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting dismissed' reads as one phrase; 'getting' is only the link. To cashier is a military term for dismissing an officer in disgrace.
explanation.definitionFit: To cashier an officer is to dismiss him from the armed forces in disgrace.

clue.text: Just over an inch needed for top design

parts.note: fair means just or equitable
in Scotland an inch is a small island

explanation.surface: A tiny bit more than an inch of material required for a top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inch' looks like a measure; in Scottish place names (Inchcolm, Inchmurrin) an inch is an island. In a down clue 'over' means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair Isle is a multicoloured knitting pattern from the Shetland island of that name, used on jumpers or tops.

clue.text: With a degree, what Bob can be: a superhero!

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a degree
a bob, or bobsleigh, can be a two-man sled

explanation.surface: With a qualification, an ordinary guy called Bob could become a superhero.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob looks like a man's name; it is a bobsleigh, raced in two-man and four-man forms.
explanation.definitionFit: Batwoman is a DC Comics superheroine allied with Batman.

clue.text: Something you will grab finally with online search?

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of the preceding word is used

parts.note: the final letter of grab
E as in e-mail stands for electronic, online
a quest is a search

explanation.surface: Something you will finally snatch with an internet search.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' is not the future tense but the verb to will, to leave in a will, and 'Something you will' is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bequest is property left to someone by will, so it is literally something you will to them.

clue.text: Education graduate's appeal for student accommodation?

parts.note: a B.Ed. is a Bachelor of Education graduate, plus the 's
it is slang for sex appeal

explanation.surface: The attractiveness of a teacher's lodgings for students.
explanation.walkthrough: A bedsit is a British single rented room used for both sleeping and living, typical of students; the question mark marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedsit is a cheap one-room flat, a typical student lodging, so it is an example of student accommodation.

clue.text: Test concentration of class descended on by singer

parts.note: a tit is a songbird, a singer
rate means class or grade, as in first-rate

explanation.surface: A test of focus for a class that a singer has visited.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'descended on by' puts the singer on top of the class. Singer is a common crossword term for a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: To titrate is to measure a solution's concentration by adding a reagent until a reaction is complete.

clue.text: Frenchman's gym slip one's put on splits

indicators.note: a word that splits is forced apart, so other letters go into its middle

parts.note: PE is physical education, the school gym lesson
I is the Roman numeral for one
to err is to slip up

explanation.surface: A French schoolgirl's gymslip being worn with a split.
explanation.walkthrough: A gymslip is a British school pinafore dress; here it splits into two words doing different jobs, and 'one's put on' means one is placed ahead of the slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre is a common French first name, so a typical Frenchman in crossword terms.

clue.text: One in a tie put up with female wearing tails, bizarrely

indicators.note: bizarrely means in a strange way, so the letters next to it are oddly reordered

parts.note: to quarter troops is to put them up in lodgings
F is the abbreviation for female
dressed in, as in 'in a hat'
the letters of tails rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone in a necktie tolerating a woman oddly dressed in a tailcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tie' suggests neckwear but is a sporting match; 'put up with' looks like 'tolerate', but 'put up' alone is the lodging verb and 'with' simply joins.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarter-finalist is a competitor taking part in one of the four matches, or ties, of a quarter-final round.

clue.text: Saw time for promotion?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old saying or proverb

explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a tool or a past tense; it is a proverb. The question mark flags the playful split: an ad is a promotion, an age a time.
explanation.definitionFit: An adage is a traditional saying, which is what a saw is in older English.

clue.text: Old scholar's letters on display at Times

parts.note: eras are times or periods
mu is a Greek letter; mus are several of them

explanation.surface: An old academic's correspondence exhibited at The Times newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' suggests correspondence, but these are Greek letters, and 'Times' is not the newspaper but periods.
explanation.definitionFit: Erasmus of Rotterdam was a Renaissance Dutch humanist, one of the great scholars of the sixteenth century.

clue.text: Lake's gold reflection portrayed by Turner

indicators.note: a mirror reflection is the image flipped, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a rotor is the turning part of a machine, a turner

explanation.surface: A lake's golden glints painted by the artist J M W Turner.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner is the painter in the surface; read literally, a turner is something that turns. AUROTOR read backwards gives the lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotorua is a lake, and town, in the volcanic region of New Zealand's North Island.

clue.text: Brother in dispute went and steered into driving place

indicators.note: into means going inside, so these pieces are placed within the next one

parts.note: golfers drive off from the tee
to wee is to urinate; went in the sense of 'went to the toilet'
to lead is to steer

explanation.surface: A sibling in a row went and drove into a parking spot.
explanation.walkthrough: WEEDLED goes inside TEE after T. Tweedledum and Tweedledee, from Lewis Carroll, agreed to have a battle over a rattle.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweedledee is one of the twin brothers in Through the Looking-Glass who quarrel over a broken rattle.

clue.text: Means to cut deal: joins in talks

indicators.note: in talks means when spoken, so the word is judged by its sound rather than spelling

parts.note: to add things is to join them

explanation.surface: A way to reach an agreement while two sides join negotiations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut a deal' suggests business; deal is pine or fir wood, and an adze is a tool for shaping timber.
explanation.definitionFit: An adze is an axe-like tool with a crosswise blade for dressing wood such as deal planks.
